name: Neck curls with plate

card.summary: Loaded forward neck flexion with a plate to thicken the neck; popular on forums, no appearance trials.
card.note: Forum users report soreness and, in one case, dizziness; no clinical data for this use.

quick.overview:
Neck curls with a plate are a weighted forward bend of the neck meant to build the muscles at the front and sides of the neck.

Forums post progress photos and debate whether the exercise affects the jaw or face. No studies have tested it for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Resistance on neck flexion works the sternocleidomastoid, which bends the neck forward when both sides contract.
quick.risks: Forum members report multi-day soreness and one reported dizziness and nausea. No clinical safety data on loaded neck curls for appearance are available.

lead: Neck curls with a plate are a form of loaded neck flexion: a person lifts or holds a weight plate on the head while bending the neck forward, aiming to thicken the muscles at the front and sides of the neck. In looksmaxxing forums the exercise is discussed as a way to build a thicker, more muscular neck and, by extension, a more masculine overall look from the shoulders up, and members post progress photos under labels such as "facial exercises".[2][4]

The sternocleidomastoid, the large muscle running from the breastbone and collarbone to the skull behind the ear, bends the neck forward when both sides contract, and it is one of the largest superficial neck muscles.[1] Wikipedia's neck article reports average neck circumference of about 38.7 cm in men and 33.3 cm in women, which it attributes mainly to differences in body composition, muscle mass and testosterone.[6] Looksmaxxing communities treat neck thickness as part of that dimorphism and train it accordingly, often alongside jaw and posture work.

Published research on loaded neck curls as an appearance exercise is not available. The related literature concerns neck strength in sports-injury prevention, neck-pain rehabilitation and posture, and training logs on strength forums show neck work as routine accessory training.[7][8][9][11]

chain: Resistance on neck flexion loads the sternocleidomastoid and neighbouring muscles
Progressive loading over weeks of training adds muscle size
Thicker neck that fills out the collar and frames the jawline
angle.text: Members use plate neck curls as hypertrophy work for the front of the neck, aiming for a wider, more muscular neck that makes the head and jaw look better supported. The visible change comes from muscle gained in the neck region, as with any other resistance exercise.

infobox: Weight plate, towel or pad; a neck harness is another option[7]
Sets of about 20 in one log[8]
Neck extensions, neck harness work, chin tucks, bridging[4][7][14]
Thicker neck; sometimes jaw and facial claims[4]

paras: The sternocleidomastoid runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process behind the ear, and bends the neck forward when both sides contract together.[1] Loaded neck curls place resistance on this movement, typically by holding a plate against the forehead or head.

Acting alone, one sternocleidomastoid turns the head to the opposite side and tilts it toward its own side, while both together flex the neck forward and help with forced inhalation.[1] It is supplied mainly by the accessory nerve, and because it is thick it divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.[1] Wikipedia's neck article places the sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and scalenes in the posterior triangle, with the trapezius forming the sloping outline between neck and shoulder.[6] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists a defined jawline among features that communities judge when rating attractiveness, which is one reason neck and jaw work are often discussed together.[10]

Neck circumference is a visible marker of upper-body muscle. Wikipedia attributes the roughly 5 cm average difference between men and women to body composition, muscle mass and testosterone, which promotes muscle growth including in the neck.[6] The same article notes that the Adam's apple is usually more prominent in men and that neck lines develop in adulthood from sun damage, weight or ageing.[6] The posterior and lateral muscles also shape the line from ear to shoulder, which is why trapezius and neck-extension work often appear in the same routines as curls.[6][7]

Wikipedia's article on forward head posture describes a head carried forward of the shoulders with a poked-forward chin, and lists strengthening of the deep neck flexors, shoulder-blade retractors and middle and lower back among suggested approaches, while noting several of these recommendations are tagged as needing independent confirmation.[13] Members who combine neck curls with chin tucks often frame both as posture and jaw-definition work.[4]

Training logs on T Nation, a strength-training forum, show neck work in several forms: one log lists a neck harness and neck curls in a daily circuit, another programmes "neck curls/extensions" for 3 sets of 20 repetitions in a hypertrophy circuit, and a poster suggests lifters do some neck curl or bridge work so the neck does not look weak.[7][8][9] These examples show neck training as routine accessory work in strength communities as well as in looksmaxxing ones.

Bridging, in which a person supports body weight through the feet and head or neck, appears in wrestling, judo, jiu-jitsu and other combat sports and is also used in gymnastics, according to Wikipedia's article on the bridge exercise, which describes it mainly as a lower-back and glute exercise.[14] Wikipedia notes that a larger neck circumference is associated with cardiometabolic risk and that upper-body fat is considered a worse predictor than lower-body fat; it does not discuss neck training.[6]

Neck strength has been studied mainly in sport. A 2021 scoping review of 11 studies on physical conditioning to reduce concussion risk, mostly in adolescents, examined neck strength, neck size and cervical stiffness as modifiable risk factors and found limited and conflicting evidence from small samples.[11] A 2024 study of 380 adult amateur soccer players found that neck strength and head and neck dimensions did not moderate the link between heading exposure and cognitive performance.[12] These studies concern injury prevention rather than appearance.

Conditions of the sternocleidomastoid include torticollis, in which overactive contraction tilts the head and physiotherapy stretches the affected side and strengthens the opposite side.[1] Wikipedia lists whiplash, cervical disc herniation, spinal stenosis and vascular causes among common sources of neck pain.[6] In looksmaxxing forums, members report multi-day soreness after resuming neck curls, and one poster described dizziness, nausea and chills after two sets, with replies suggesting reflux as a possible cause.[3][5] No clinical data on loaded neck curls for appearance are available; forum reports are individual accounts.

Members post before-and-after photos attributed to neck curls and ask how long the person trained.[2] Beginners describe sets of around twenty repetitions as exhausting, and one member reports several days of soreness when turning the head after resuming the exercise.[3] Others ask whether curls enlarge the trapezius as well as the sternocleidomastoid.[3]

Several threads ask whether neck curls and chin tucks help the jaw or face, with participants disagreeing about whether they are useful.[4] Looksmaxxing as a whole, as described by Wikipedia, spans skincare and gym training through to cosmetic surgery, and exercise-based methods such as neck work sit at the low-cost end of that range.[10]

No studies found. Related research on neck strength in sports-injury prevention and on cervical exercise for pain exists, but no trial has tested weighted neck curls for neck size or facial appearance.[11][12]

lore.intro: Neck curls are discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a facial-adjacent exercise, often grouped with chin tucks [4].

claims.claim: Neck curls produce visible progress in neck and facial appearance
claims.believers: Posters share before-and-after images under the label 'facial exercises' and receive admiring replies [2].
claims.experts: No published studies have tested loaded neck curls for facial appearance.

claims.claim: Neck curls and chin tucks widen the jaw or improve the face
claims.believers: Multiple threads ask whether the pair helps the jaw, with some members presenting them as helpful [4].
claims.experts: No published studies have examined whether these exercises change jaw width or facial structure.

claims.claim: Starting neck curls too hard can cause soreness or other symptoms
claims.believers: Users report multi-day soreness [3] and, in one case, dizziness, headache and chills after two sets [5].
claims.experts: No clinical data on loaded neck curls in this setting are available; these are individual forum reports.

claims.claim: A thicker neck makes the whole physique look stronger.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster says working the neck gives the effect of looking strong, even for someone with a good body, and that the neck can signal weakness or strength.[9]
claims.experts: Average neck size differs between men and women, which Wikipedia attributes to body composition, muscle mass and testosterone; no study tested neck training for perceived physique.[6]

claims.claim: A thicker neck makes the jaw look stronger and the head look better supported
claims.believers: Members who post neck progress photos describe the neck as part of the lower-face frame.[2][4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia's neck article links neck size differences between the sexes to muscle mass and testosterone; no study has examined neck training and perceived jaw strength.[6]

claims.believers: Strength-forum posters treat neck work as routine accessory training and say it stops the neck looking weak.[9]
claims.experts: A 2021 scoping review found limited and conflicting evidence on neck strength and concussion risk, and a 2024 study of soccer heading found no moderating effect.[11][12]

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck flexor work fix forward head posture
claims.believers: Forum members pair chin tucks with neck curls as posture and jaw exercises.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists deep neck flexor strengthening among approaches for forward head posture and notes that some recommendations lack independent confirmation.[13]
